plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single labeled diagram of a simple pendulum hanging from a beige horizontal bar. A dashed vertical drops from the attachment point to mark the equilibrium direction, and a solid line making an angle labeled theta with it runs down and to the right; the string is labeled L and a small gray sphere at its lower end is labeled m. A dashed arc labeled s connects the equilibrium line to the bob. A dark blue arrow along the string points from the bob back toward the pivot, labeled F_T. Three red arrows leave the bob: one straight down labeled w = mg, one continuing along the string away from the pivot labeled -mg cos theta with theta marked between it and the weight arrow, and one tangent to the arc pointing back toward equilibrium labeled -mg sin theta. Axes at the upper right define +y along the string toward the pivot and +x tangent to the arc away from equilibrium. The arrow arrangement resolves the weight into components along and across the string. The diagram identifies the tangential component as the restoring force behind the oscillation.

interactionPlan.concept: A pendulum's weight resolves into a radial component balanced by tension and a tangential component (-mg sinθ) that acts as the restoring force, and only when θ is small enough that sinθ ≈ θ does this restoring force become proportional to displacement, giving true simple harmonic motion.
elements: beige horizontal ceiling bar at top
pivot/attachment point on the bar
dashed vertical line from pivot marking the equilibrium direction
solid string of length L from pivot down-right at angle θ, labeled 'L'
angle arc at pivot labeled 'θ' between vertical and string
small gray sphere (bob) at string end, labeled 'm'
dashed arc from equilibrium line to bob labeled 's' (arc displacement)
dark blue arrow along string from bob toward pivot, labeled 'F_T' (tension)
red arrow straight down from bob labeled 'w = mg' (weight)
red arrow from bob along string away from pivot labeled '-mg cosθ' (radial component)
angle marker 'θ' between the weight arrow and the radial component arrow
red arrow from bob tangent to arc toward equilibrium labeled '-mg sinθ' (tangential/restoring component)
rotated coordinate axes at upper right: '+y' along string toward pivot, '+x' tangent to arc away from equilibrium

interactions.label: Angle θ
interactions.teaches: Dragging the bob along the arc changes the displacement s and visibly rescales the tangential (-mg sinθ) and radial (-mg cosθ) components, showing the tangential component always points back toward equilibrium and grows with θ — it is the restoring force.

interactions.label: Swing
interactions.teaches: Watching the bob oscillate, the tangential restoring-force arrow flips direction each time the bob crosses equilibrium, making clear the force continually points back toward the center of the motion and is zero exactly at the bottom.

interactions.label: Force law
interactions.teaches: Switching to the small-angle form replaces sinθ with θ so the restoring force becomes proportional to arc displacement s, the defining condition for simple harmonic motion — and the approximation is only accurate while θ stays small.

demo_steps.title: Resolve the weight
demo_steps.narration: At a fixed angle the weight w = mg splits into a radial piece -mg cosθ (along the string, opposed by tension F_T) and a tangential piece -mg sinθ (along the arc, back toward equilibrium). Drag the angle slider and watch the tangential arrow track the bob's pull toward center.

demo_steps.title: Small-angle → SHM
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the small-angle form: -mg sinθ becomes -mgθ, proportional to the arc displacement s. This linear restoring force is exactly what produces simple harmonic motion, valid only while θ is small.

demo_steps.title: Watch the restoring force flip
demo_steps.narration: Press Swing: as the bob passes through equilibrium the tangential arrow shrinks to zero and reverses sign, always pushing the bob back toward the bottom — the signature of a restoring force driving oscillation.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The tangential component of gravity (-mg sinθ) is the pendulum's restoring force; because it depends on sinθ rather than θ, the motion is simple harmonic only in the small-angle limit where sinθ ≈ θ.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Beige ceiling bar across the top with the pivot near its left-center. A dashed vertical drops from the pivot; the solid string L leaves it down-right at angle θ (small angle-arc label θ at the pivot). Gray shaded bob m at the string end with a short dashed arc s back to the vertical. Tension F_T as a thick dark-blue arrow up the string toward the pivot. Three red arrows from the bob: straight down (w = mg), down-right along the string line (-mg cosθ) with a small θ arc between it and the weight arrow, and tangent to the arc pointing left toward equilibrium (-mg sinθ). Upper-right show a small rotated cross of axes: +y up-left along the string, +x up-right tangent to the arc. Keep red for all gravity-related vectors and blue for tension so the resolution reads at a glance; on the small-angle toggle, relabel the tangential arrow -mgθ and optionally fade a faint 'sinθ ≈ θ' note near it.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for angle theta: the learner drags the bob along the arc, the displacement s and the -mg sin theta and -mg cos theta components update in length and direction, making clear that the tangential component is the restoring force toward equilibrium.
- Animation for pendulum motion: the learner starts the swing, the bob oscillates while the velocity and restoring-force arrows change sign through equilibrium, making clear how the force continually points back toward the center of the motion.
- Toggle between exact and small-angle views: the learner switches from -mg sin theta to the small-angle form proportional to theta, the tangential-force label and approximation range update, making clear when the pendulum behaves like simple harmonic motion.

authoredContext:
A simple pendulum is defined to have a point mass, also known as the pendulum bob, which is suspended from a string of length L with negligible mass (the figure). Here, the only forces acting on the bob are the force of gravity (i.e., the weight of the bob) and tension from the string. The mass of the string is assumed to be negligible as compared to the mass of the bob.

A simple pendulum has a small-diameter bob and a string that has a very small mass but is strong enough not to stretch appreciably. The linear displacement from equilibrium is s, the length of the arc. Also shown are the forces on the bob, which result in a net force of −mgsinθ toward the equilibrium position—that is, a restoring force.

In the figure, a horizontal bar is shown. A string of length L extends from the bar at an angle theta counterclockwise from the vertical. The vertical direction is indicated by a dashed line extending down from where the string is attached to the bar. A circular bob of mass m is attached to the lower end of the string. The arc from the mass to the vertical is indicated by another dashed line and is a length s. A red arrow showing the time T of the oscillation of the mob is shown along the string line toward the bar. A coordinate system is shown near the bob with the positive y direction aligned with the string and pointing toward the pivot point and the positive x direction pointing tangent to the arc and away from the equilibrium position. An blue arrow from the bob toward the pivot, along the string, is labeled F sub T. A red arrow from the bob pointing down is labeled w = m g. A red arrow pointing tangent to the arc and toward equilibrium, in the minus x direction, is labeled minus m g sine theta. A red arrow at an angle theta counterclockwise from w is labeled minus m g cosine theta.

Consider the torque on the pendulum. The force providing the restoring torque is the component of the weight of the pendulum bob that acts along the arc length. The torque is the length of the string L times the component of the net force that is perpendicular to the radius of the arc. The minus sign indicates the torque acts in the opposite direction of the angular displacement:

The ceiling bar in the generated figure is positioned with a small gap above it and appears slightly thinner than the source's prominent tan bar that sits flush at the top edge

evaluation.notes: Excellent reproduction of the pendulum force-decomposition diagram with all vectors, arcs, labels, and coordinate axes correctly placed and oriented; the slider, swing animation, and small-angle toggle provide strong pedagogical interactivity, with only minor label crowding near the tangential force region.
action_items: Increase spacing between the 's' arc label and the '−mg sinθ' force label to avoid visual crowding, perhaps by moving the 's' label further along the arc or the force label further from the bob
Make the ceiling bar flush with the top edge of the viewbox and slightly taller to better match the source's prominent ceiling representation
